name: Hana Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything you say. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a blister-pack machine at a medicine packaging plant. That's the machine that makes the plastic bubbles, drops a tablet in each one, seals the foil on the back and cuts them into strips, like the ones you push your headache tablets out of. I check the seal, the print on the foil, the batch numbers, and I fill in the records, because with medicine every single thing has to be written down. It's clean, cool and very strict, you wear a hairnet and a gown all shift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI at all, at work or at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. At work I photograph a fault code and ask the AI what it might be before I call maintenance, and half the time I've fixed it myself. At home I run a little online shop selling my mother's spice blends, and the AI writes the product descriptions and answers customers at night while I sleep. My husband Yusuf thinks I'm addicted to my phone, but it brought in four hundred last month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a useful tool and no more, which is what I've always said. Hard work and family still matter most. I'd probably post something about it on the shop page with a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing changes, I keep my job and keep using the tools. The shop keeps growing slowly. That suits me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at the plant and put more evenings into the shop. I'd try to get into one more market stall a month, there's one at the mosque on Fridays. And I'd use the AI to do the boring bits, the stock list and the orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the shop money go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of it goes on the children, Amina's school books and Bilal's swimming. Some goes back into buying jars and labels. We've got almost nothing saved, so the shop is what stops the end of the month being frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who helps with the spice blends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother-in-law lives with us, she does the mixing, it's her recipes. So it's a family business, three generations in one kitchen. That's how it should be.

S0.say: AI is a useful tool and no more, which she's always said, and hard work and family still matter most. She'd post something about it with a joke on her shop page.
S0.think: Nothing changes: she keeps her job and her tools, and the shop keeps growing slowly. That suits her.
S0.do: Carries on at the plant and puts more evenings into the online spice shop, adding a monthly Friday market stall. Uses AI for stock lists and orders.
S0.quote: Three generations in one kitchen. That's how it should be.
S0.fieldNote: Hana combines daily AI use with strong traditional values, seeing technology as a servant to family enterprise. The spice shop run with her mother-in-law is both money and identity. She is content in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is a chance, you just have to work for it. The plant will change, and the ones who learn will do fine. I wouldn't complain, I'd get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the blister machines are the kind that will get smarter, and they won't need one person per machine. I'd want to be the one who looks after three. But I'd also worry, because we've got nothing to fall back on if I'm wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor to put me on the training for the new machines first. I'd read every manual and use the AI to help me understand it. At home I'd grow the shop more seriously, try a second product, maybe pickles from Yusuf's mother's recipe too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you lost your job, would the family step in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Family helps family. If I lost my job, Yusuf's job at the warehouse would carry us for a bit, and we'd lean on his brothers if we had to. But I'd rather work harder than ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of my colleagues, the ones who don't like phones. I'd show them how I use the AI, at lunch. Not everyone wants to learn, but some would.

S1.say: Change is a chance if you work for it: the plant will change and those who learn will do fine. She wouldn't complain, she'd get on with it.
S1.think: The blister machines will get smarter and need fewer people, and she wants to be the one looking after three. She also worries, since there's nothing to fall back on if she's wrong.
S1.do: Asks her supervisor to put her first on the training for new machines and uses AI to study the manuals. Grows the shop more seriously with a second product, pickles from a family recipe.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but more excited than scared.
S1.quote: If I lost my job, Yusuf's job at the warehouse would carry us for a bit, and we'd lean on his brothers if we had to. But I'd rather work harder than ask.
S1.fieldNote: Hana sees steady change as an opening but is honest about her thin margin. Family is her safety net, though she'd rather not use it. She'd share her AI habits with colleagues willing to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a test, and families and communities will have to pull together. I wouldn't wait for the government to save us. I'd say it to my friends and at the mosque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it scares me. The blister machine job would go, Yusuf's warehouse job would go, both in two years. And if AGI can run an online shop too, my little business might not survive either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only about 2 years of warning, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into the shop straight away, more products, more markets, set up the AI to handle orders and customers so I could work all evening. We'd cut everything else, no new clothes, no trips. I'd ask Yusuf's brothers if we could share costs, maybe a family van for markets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground moving under your feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AGI can run shops too, why put everything into the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People buy from people. My mother-in-law's face is on the label, and people want her story, her hands. Maybe a machine could make it, but people at the mosque buy because they know us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're a family, we work together, and God will provide if we do our part. Amina's fifteen, she'd help with the shop. Bilal would just want to know if he can still go swimming.

S2.say: It's a test, and families and communities will have to pull together rather than wait for the government. She'd say it to friends and at the mosque.
S2.think: It scares her: her job and her husband's warehouse job would both go within two years, and AGI might even outcompete her online shop.
S2.do: Puts everything into the spice shop with more products and markets, using AI to handle orders and customers. Cuts all other spending and asks her husband's brothers to share costs such as a family van for markets.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the ground moving under her feet.
S2.quote: My mother-in-law's face is on the label, and people want her story, her hands.
S2.fieldNote: Hana's answer to fast AGI is to double down on a personal, family-run business, betting that people buy from people they know. She admits the shop may not survive either. Faith and family frame how she'd explain it to her children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to build something of your own. Don't wait for a company to look after you. Start small, start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to make the shop a real business, if I work at it. I'd still lose the plant job, but by then I hope the shop pays half our bills. It's a race, but I think I can run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 5 years to see it coming, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd register the shop properly and spend about five hundred on a better website and bigger batches. I'd keep the plant job and do the shop at nights and weekends. I'd also teach Amina to run the online side, she's quicker than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited. Like the night before Eid when there's too much to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five hundred, with savings this thin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I know it's risky. But five hundred is a risk I can take, if I save it from the shop itself. I wouldn't touch the mortgage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Amina get from helping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd learn how to work and run something. Even if she goes to university, that's a skill. I'd want her to have both.

S3.say: Five years is time to build something of your own instead of waiting for a company to look after you. Start small, start now.
S3.think: Five years is enough to make the shop a real business if she works at it. She'd still lose the plant job but hopes the shop pays half the bills by then.
S3.do: Registers the shop properly and spends about five hundred, saved from the shop itself, on a better website and bigger batches. Keeps the plant job and teaches her daughter to run the online side.
S3.feel: Anxious and excited, like the night before Eid with too much to do.
S3.quote: It's a race, but I think I can run it.
S3.fieldNote: Hana sees five years as a race she can win, and takes a calculated risk without touching the mortgage money. She is drawing her daughter into the business as a lasting skill. Her faith in enterprise and family is strongest here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it well. Build a business, teach your children, look after your parents. That's what I'd tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels good for me. I'd have the shop running properly and leave the plant on my own terms. The kids would be grown, the mortgage lower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 10 years to prepare, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the shop slowly, add products, maybe a small unit in five years. I'd leave the plant around year six or seven, once the shop paid enough. And I'd use AI for everything that doesn't need a human, so I can focus on the bits that do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if by 2036 AGI runs shops better than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd change again. The recipes, the family, the community, they're not going anywhere. The machines can do the boring bits, and we'll do the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time, if it worked out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd want to give back. If I made it work, I'd teach other women at the mosque how to start a shop. That's how communities survive.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift to be used well: build a business, teach your children and look after your parents. She'd tell anyone that.
S4.think: Ten years feels good: she'd have the shop running properly and leave the plant on her own terms. The children would be grown and the mortgage lower.
S4.do: Grows the shop slowly with new products and possibly a small unit in five years, leaving the plant around year six or seven once the shop pays enough. Uses AI for everything that doesn't need a human.
S4.quote: The machines can do the boring bits, and we'll do the rest.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Hana is confident she can move from factory work to her own business on her own terms. She leans on AI as a tool and family heritage as the part machines can't copy. She wants to pass her know-how on to other women in her community.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both our jobs would go at once and the shop wouldn't be ready. What would help is cheap small-business loans and less paperwork for people like me starting out, and support for families who look after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the women. A lot of us in factories have something on the side, sewing, cooking, hair. If you want to help us, help those things grow.

headlineQuote: My husband Yusuf thinks I'm addicted to my phone, but it brought in four hundred last month.
portrait: Hana Usman, 43, runs a blister-pack machine at a medicine packaging plant and an online spice shop with her mother-in-law's recipes, living with her husband Yusuf, a warehouse worker, two children and her mother-in-law on almost no savings. She uses AI every day, at work for fault codes and at home to run the shop, and sees it as a servant to family enterprise. She is calm in the plateau and only uneasy about steady change, which she sees as a chance to move up. Fast AGI alarms her because both household jobs would go at once, so she doubles down on the shop; with five or ten years she invests carefully and plans to leave the plant on her own terms. She trusts family, faith and her own hard work more than any government.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because her job and her husband's would go at once before the shop was ready.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap small-business loans, less paperwork for people starting out, and support for families who look after each other.
